analysis.one_liner: Shields hospitals, nursing homes, pharmacies, and food businesses from most COVID-related lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee after being referred there on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have said that hospitals, nursing homes, clinics, pharmacies, farms, meatpacking and food processing plants, restaurants, and grocery stores cannot be sued for harm caused by exposure to or infection with COVID-19 during the pandemic emergency. The shield covers federal and state claims and overrides state laws, unless a state gives businesses even more protection. The only way around it is to prove willful misconduct, gross negligence, recklessness, or conscious flagrant indifference — a high bar for an injured worker or patient. The bill never advanced past its referral to the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, health care facilities (including nursing homes) and every link of the food chain — farms, processors, packagers, restaurants, and grocers — would have been immune from most civil lawsuits over COVID exposure, and their insurers would have paid far fewer claims. Businesses could not be sued for ordinary negligence, such as failing to protect workers or residents from the virus; plaintiffs would have to clear the much higher threshold of gross negligence or worse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, food businesses, insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars liability under federal or state law for any act or omission by a covered provider that causes harm arising from exposure to or infection by COVID-19 during the declared public health emergency.

Covered providers include health care entities — nursing homes, clinics, pharmacies, hospitals, outpatient centers, blood donation centers, and urgent care centers — and food providers, including farms, fisheries, food processing and packaging plants, restaurants, and grocery stores.

It preempts state law wherever state rules are less protective of businesses, and it does not apply only where harm resulted from willful or criminal misconduct, gross negligence, reckless misconduct, or conscious flagrant indifference.

analysis.who_pays: People who caught COVID-19 in a nursing home, hospital, workplace, restaurant, or grocery store, and their families, would bear the cost of their own injuries: someone harmed by ordinary negligence — a nursing home that failed to isolate sick residents, a meatpacking plant that crowded workers — would have no lawsuit unless they could prove gross negligence or worse, which is a demanding standard. State courts and juries, which normally decide these cases, would also lose authority over them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured patients, nursing home residents, and workers

drawbacks.text: Ordinary negligence would go uncompensated: the bill's exception requires showing willful or criminal misconduct, gross negligence, reckless misconduct, or conscious flagrant indifference, a far higher bar than the negligence standard injured people would normally sue under.
Nursing homes were central to COVID deaths among elderly residents, and a blanket shield with a narrow exception would leave families of residents harmed by ordinary care failures without recourse.
The bill would override state tort law, taking these disputes away from state courts and juries even in states that wanted to keep full liability rules.

Supporters would argue that hospitals and essential food businesses faced unprecedented emergency conditions and unforeseeable lawsuit risk during the pandemic; the bill's carve-outs for gross negligence and worse were an attempt to answer that concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to businesses and their insurers, who would have been shielded from costly litigation during a crisis; the cost runs to the people actually harmed by COVID exposure, who would lose their main legal remedy for ordinary negligence. Even with the gross-negligence exception, the bill would have shifted the burden of pandemic injuries from the facilities involved to the injured and, ultimately, to public programs and families. It also raises the fair point that front-line facilities operated under extreme uncertainty, but a broad preemptive shield with only a gross-negligence carve-out goes well beyond protecting good-faith emergency decisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gregory Murphy introduced the bill on June 11, 2020, with Rep. Andy Harris as an original cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died, nursing home residents, hospital patients, and essential workers kept their existing right to sue under ordinary negligence rules, and health care and food businesses gained nothing beyond the protections already in state law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients and workers, who kept their right to sue

for.name: Rep. Gregory Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Pandemic Liability Protection Act and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were House Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors; the Democratic-controlled committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Nursing homes were a leading site of COVID deaths, and the bill would have barred suits by residents' families for ordinary negligence, leaving only the much harder gross-negligence standard. The industry's gain is injured families' loss.
These providers would be immune from most COVID-related malpractice and negligence suits under federal and state law. Patients harmed by ordinary care failures would have no claim.

industries.industry: Food supply chain (farms, meatpacking and food processing, packaging, restaurants, grocery stores)
industries.note: Essential food workers and customers exposed to the virus at these businesses could not sue for ordinary negligence. The cost of workplace and customer infections would fall on the injured and public programs instead.
A near-blanket immunity shield would sharply reduce pandemic-related claims paid by business insurers. Businesses' savings would come directly out of compensation otherwise owed to injured people.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' trial bar and injured persons
industries.note: The bill would eliminate most COVID-related civil suits, removing the main legal avenue for workers, patients, and families to recover for negligent exposure. Its death preserved that avenue.
